name: Freya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Freya, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how would you describe your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm assistant manager at Hartley Farms, which is owned by a food company, not a family. We've got four free-range egg sheds, about 32,000 hens, a beef finishing unit, and a lot of wheat and oilseed rape. There are eight of us full-time plus contractors at harvest. I've been there eleven years, and before that I was on a dairy farm near my parents'.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven o'clock I'm in the egg sheds, checking the birds, the ventilation, the egg belts, anything dead or poorly. Mid-morning I do rotas and orders, then I'm usually out on the sprayer or checking crops. Joel says I live in my wellies. I like that every day's different and I'm trusted to make calls. What wears me out is the audits; the company sends someone with a clipboard every quarter, and the welfare paperwork never ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it turned out to be another tool, like GPS steering was. Useful, not magic. I'd say that at work and to my sister, who's convinced it's all going to end the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, steady as you go. The company keeps the farm, I keep the job, and my pay's good for farm work. That's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd keep using the AI for the audit reports, maybe a bit more. Keep putting a bit into savings and the shares Joel and I hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's pretty much how I'd guess it goes, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing up the welfare reports and the monthly summary for the company. I type my notes in, it makes them tidy. I only started after the other manager, Rhys, had used it for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd want to change in your own work, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less paperwork, more time with the birds. If AI could do the audits for me I'd be happy. Not much else.

S0.say: I'd say it turned out to be another tool, like GPS steering, useful but not magic. I'd say that at work and to my worried sister.
S0.think: For me it's steady as you go: the company keeps the farm and I keep a well-paid job. That's fine by me.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal and uses AI a bit more for audit reports. Keeps saving and holding shares with her partner.
S0.quote: If AI could do the audits for me I'd be happy.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is measured and practical, comparing AI to GPS steering. She picked up AI tools after a colleague proved them. Her main wish is less paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change we've seen before, and we'll manage. I'd want the company to be straight with us about what's coming. I'm not one for big posts online, but I'd say it at the staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be OK, maybe better off. Someone's got to run the robot shed cleaners and the egg grading machines, and I'm the one who already sorts the computer side. But I'd be doing less hands-on, and I'd miss it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for training on the new systems as soon as they're on another site and working. I'd use the AI tools more for rotas and reports. And I'd keep saving as normal, no big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small knot about the team. I'd feel it most on the days the engineers came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Hartley would feel this most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dean, who does the sheds. He's lovely, and he's slow with tech. If they bring in robot egg collection, he's the one at risk. I'd try to keep him on the bits that need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another farm if the company went too far with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly, there's work around here. But Hartley pays better than the family farms, and I've got the kids' schools and the mortgage here. I'd rather adapt than move.

S1.say: I'd say it's change we've seen before and we'll manage. I'd want the company to be straight about what's coming and say so at the staff meeting.
S1.think: I think I'd be OK, maybe better off, because I already handle the computer side. But I'd be doing less hands-on work and I'd miss it.
S1.do: Asks the company for training on new systems once they work on another site. Uses AI tools more for rotas and reports and keeps saving as normal.
S1.feel: Calm, with a small knot of worry for her team.
S1.fieldNote: Freya sees herself as the person who bridges the old and new systems. Her worry is for a colleague who is slow with tech. She'd stay put because Hartley pays well and her family is settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, and fast. Not panic, a plan. I'd probably say it in the parents' group too, because everyone would be talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Hartley would go robotic fast. They're a company, they'd do the sums. I'd be one of the last people there, but I'd still go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any big spending, we were going to do the bathroom next year. I'd keep the savings in cash, not shares, in case the market goes mad. And I'd talk to Mia about whether university still makes sense, she's fifteen and wants to do nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still be getting up and doing the job, but I'd be watching the company emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What does that short warning do to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel's job would last a bit longer, robots still need wiring, at least at first. So we'd have one wage for a while. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Joel's an electrician. Does that change the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no time to see what works for other people first. That's how I usually do it, wait for Rhys or the farm down the road, then copy. With two years, I'd just be guessing.

S2.say: I'd say we need a plan from the government, and fast, not panic but a plan. I'd say it in the parents' group too.
S2.think: I think Hartley would go robotic fast because they're a company and they'd do the sums. I'd be one of the last there, but I'd still go.
S2.do: Holds off on the planned bathroom and moves savings from shares into cash. Talks with her daughter about whether university nursing still makes sense.
S2.feel: Anxious but still functioning, watching company emails.
S2.quote: They're a company, they'd do the sums. I'd be one of the last people there, but I'd still go.
S2.fieldNote: Freya stays practical even here, moving money to cash and reviewing family plans. Her partner's electrical trade gives her some comfort. The speed bothers her mainly because she usually waits to copy proven moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's get ready properly. Training, a safety net, the lot. I'd say it to the company and at the farmers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe three or four more years at Hartley, then something else. Five years is enough to sort myself out, just about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on any training the company offers for running robot systems in the first year or two. I'd save harder, an extra three hundred a month. And I'd help the kids plan their studies around what's still going to be needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd feel more in charge. I can work with a deadline I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to see how other farms do it and copy the bits that work. That's my way. With five years I've got time to watch and then move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia and Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to pick something they love, and something with people in it. Mia wants nursing, Ben wants to be a vet. I'd say go for it, but keep an eye on what the machines can do.

S3.say: I'd say it's coming, so let's get ready properly with training and a safety net. I'd say it to the company and at the farmers' meeting.
S3.think: I think I'd get three or four more years at Hartley, then something else. Five years is just about enough to sort myself out.
S3.do: Takes company training on robot systems in the first year or two and saves an extra 300 a month. Helps the children plan studies around work that will still be needed.
S3.quote: With five years I've got time to watch and then move.
S3.fieldNote: Freya's steady approach works with five years: she can watch others, then move. She talks to her children about choosing work with people in it. She remains pragmatic and doesn't blame anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this well. Let's not rush and let's not ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be in my fifties, mortgage nearly done, kids grown. I'd still lose the job eventually, though, and that bothers me more than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year, not much. I'd keep using the AI tools and keep saving. In three or four years, once it's clear which way it's going, I'd train in something new, maybe managing robot farm systems or something to do with animal welfare checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but a long way off. It's a worry for the back of the drawer, not the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What would you start in the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. That's my weakness, waiting for proof. But ten years is long enough that even I would see it coming in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to stay in farming somehow. Even if a robot does the work, someone has to decide what's grown and how the animals are kept.

S4.say: I'd say there's time to do this well, so let's not rush and let's not ignore it. That's my line at work and at home.
S4.think: I'd be fine, in my fifties with the mortgage nearly done and the kids grown. I'd still lose the job eventually, and that bothers me more than I'd say out loud.
S4.do: Keeps using AI tools and saving in the first year. Retrains in three or four years, perhaps in managing robot farm systems or animal welfare checks, once the direction is clear.
S4.feel: A distant unease, more than she'd show.
S4.quote: Someone has to decide what's grown and how the animals are kept.
S4.fieldNote: Freya knows her weakness is waiting for proof but trusts that ten years is enough even for her. She'd want to stay in farming in a deciding role. Her private worry is bigger than her public calm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I need to see how it goes for others before I move. What would help is a clear plan from government, retraining that's paid for, and some guarantee for farm workers so it's not just the company deciding.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the animals. Robots can collect eggs, but I'd want to know who's checking that the hens are all right. That's the bit I'd fight for.

headlineQuote: Robots can collect eggs, but I'd want to know who's checking that the hens are all right.
portrait: Freya Silva is a 43-year-old assistant manager at Hartley Farms, a company-owned egg, beef and arable farm, married to Joel, an electrician, with two children. She's practical, well paid and has savings and shares, and she adopts tools once a colleague has proved them. She stays calm when AI stalls or changes things steadily and becomes anxious with AGI in two years, mainly because there's no time to watch and copy. With five or ten years she trains for robot systems and helps her children plan. She cares deeply about animal welfare.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she needs to see how change goes for others before she moves.
whatWouldHelp: A clear government plan, paid retraining, and guarantees for farm workers so the company isn't the only one deciding.
